## 1. Purpose

This module compares three genomic best linear unbiased prediction
(GBLUP) structures from [R04A](real_data_gblup.html) and four
artificial neural-network (ANN) variants from
[R04B](real_data_ann.html). All seven methods predict the same
precomputed individual phenotypic BLUPs using the common outer
cross-validation design established in
[R03](real_data_validation.html). The stored results are read directly;
no genomic prediction model is refitted in this module.

| Model | Genomic structure or explicit weight penalty |
|:------|:---------------------------------------------|
| GBLUP_A | Additive genomic relationship |
| GBLUP_AD | Additive and dominance genomic relationships |
| GBLUP_ADE | Additive, dominance and additive-by-additive epistatic genomic relationships |
| ANN_0 | No explicit L1 or L2 penalty |
| ANN_L1 | L1 weight penalty |
| ANN_L2 | L2 weight penalty |
| ANN_L1_L2 | Simultaneous L1 and L2 weight penalties |

All four ANN variants use early stopping during the selection of
training duration. ANN_0 therefore denotes the absence of explicit
L1 and L2 penalties, not the absence of every form of regularization.
The GBLUP structures use their respective genomic relationship matrices,
whereas the ANN variants use genomic markers as network inputs.

The population comprises 195 individuals evaluated for Cer, BM and LP.
Five repetitions of five-fold outer cross-validation yield 25
assessment splits per trait and model, each with 39 held-out individuals.
The ANN hyperparameters were selected within the corresponding outer
analysis samples in R04B; GBLUP uses the three prespecified structures
in R04A.

Unlike the simulated analysis, the real data do not provide known true
genetic values. The evaluation target is the phenotypic BLUP, which was
estimated before the genomic validation design and was not refitted
within each genomic split. Agreement with these BLUPs therefore measures
genomic prediction of the available phenotypic reference, not accuracy
against known true genetic values. Throughout this module, GEBV denotes
the stored genomic prediction on the BLUP scale; it does not imply
that the full prediction is an additive breeding value for every model.

The comparison distinguishes three scientific questions:

- How well does each model predict the phenotypic BLUP within an outer
  assessment split? Pearson, Spearman, RMSE and MAE are the primary
  metrics; bias and calibration slope provide complementary information.
- How do the models differ on matched outer splits?
- How well do the mean out-of-fold (OOF) predictions recover individual
  rankings and the upper 20% of the phenotypic BLUP distribution, and
  how similar are the ranking strata produced by different models?

Repeated cross-validation reuses individuals across analysis sets and
assessment repetitions. The split-level summaries and contrasts are
descriptive, not significance tests based on 25 independent replicates.

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE,
  warning = FALSE,
  message = FALSE,
  cache = FALSE,
  fig.align = "center",
  out.width = "100%"
)

COMPARISON_DIR <- "output/real/comparison"

FIGURE_DIR <- file.path(COMPARISON_DIR, "figures")

dir.create(COMPARISON_DIR, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

dir.create(FIGURE_DIR, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
```

## 2. Prediction data and cross-validation

### 2.1 Packages and dependencies

The module uses `knitr` and `kableExtra` for tables and `ggplot2` with
`ggthemes` for figures. The stored fitting outputs are sufficient for
the comparison; neither BGLR nor torch is required here.

```{r packages}
library(knitr)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggthemes)
```

### 2.2 Saved prediction results and validation design

The six fitting outputs have three different units of observation.
The validation design from R03 supplies the assessment identifiers
against which their coverage is examined.

| Input object | Unit of observation | Expected rows |
|:-------------|:--------------------|--------------:|
| gblup_results | Trait, outer split and GBLUP structure | 225 |
| ann_results | Trait, outer split and ANN variant | 300 |
| gblup_predictions | Held-out individual, trait, outer split and GBLUP structure | 8,775 |
| ann_predictions | Held-out individual, trait, outer split and ANN variant | 11,700 |
| gblup_ranking | Individual, trait and GBLUP structure | 1,755 |
| ann_ranking | Individual, trait and ANN variant | 2,340 |

```{r read-model-predictions}
gblup_results <- readRDS("output/real/gblup/real_gblup_results.rds")

gblup_predictions <- readRDS("output/real/gblup/real_gblup_predictions.rds")

gblup_ranking <- readRDS("output/real/gblup/real_gblup_individual_ranking.rds")

ann_results <- readRDS("output/real/ann/final/real_ann_results.rds")

ann_predictions <- readRDS("output/real/ann/final/real_ann_predictions.rds")

ann_ranking <- readRDS("output/real/ann/final/real_ann_individual_ranking.rds")
```

The common validation object is read without regenerating folds.

```{r comparison-validation-design}
comparison_cv <- readRDS("output/real/validation/real_cv_design.rds")

comparison_assessment <- comparison_cv$outer_assignments[
  , c("Repetition", "OuterFold", "SplitID", "ID"), drop = FALSE
]
names(comparison_assessment)[
  names(comparison_assessment) == "OuterFold"
] <- "Fold"
```

### 2.3 Harmonizing the result columns and model identifiers

Both fitting modules use the same metrics and prediction targets.
The following named vectors map the original column names to the
short names used throughout this comparison. A loop applies each
mapping to the corresponding pair of data frames. Only column names
change; the stored values, row order and files remain unchanged.

```{r normalize-comparison-columns}
metric_names <- c(
  BLUP_Correlation = "Pearson", BLUP_Spearman = "Spearman",
  BLUP_RMSE = "RMSE", BLUP_MAE = "MAE",
  BLUP_Bias = "Bias", BLUP_Slope = "Slope"
)
prediction_names <- c(Observed_BLUP = "BLUP", Predicted_BLUP = "GEBV")
ranking_names <- c(
  prediction_names, Prediction_SD = "GEBV_SD",
  Observed_Rank = "BLUP_Rank", Predicted_Rank = "GEBV_Rank",
  Observed_Top20 = "BLUP_Top20", Predicted_Top20 = "GEBV_Top20"
)

# Harmonize the metric, prediction and ranking columns separately.
for (old_name in names(metric_names)) {
  names(gblup_results)[names(gblup_results) == old_name] <- metric_names[[old_name]]
  names(ann_results)[names(ann_results) == old_name] <- metric_names[[old_name]]
}

for (old_name in names(prediction_names)) {
  names(gblup_predictions)[names(gblup_predictions) == old_name] <- prediction_names[[old_name]]
  names(ann_predictions)[names(ann_predictions) == old_name] <- prediction_names[[old_name]]
}

for (old_name in names(ranking_names)) {
  names(gblup_ranking)[names(gblup_ranking) == old_name] <- ranking_names[[old_name]]
  names(ann_ranking)[names(ann_ranking) == old_name] <- ranking_names[[old_name]]
}
```

The scientific identifiers select the seven existing models. The
display labels provide a common order for tables and figures;
they do not define new model structures.

```{r compared-models}
traits <- c("Cer", "BM", "LP")

gblup_models <- c("GBLUP_A", "GBLUP_AD", "GBLUP_ADE")

ann_models <- c("ANN_0", "ANN_L1", "ANN_L2", "ANN_L1_L2")

model_order <- c(gblup_models, ann_models)

model_labels <- c("GBLUP-A", "GBLUP-AD", "GBLUP-ADE", "ANN-0", "ANN-L1", "ANN-L2", "ANN-L1+L2")

```

### 2.4 Numbers of assessments and predictions

Each model contributes 75 trait-by-split results, 2,925 held-out
predictions and 585 individual OOF ranking records. The first table
counts the two families' stored results and prediction records.
The ranking table then counts the individual records separately.

```{r input-record-counts}
input_summary <- data.frame(
  Branch = c("GBLUP", "ANN"),
  Models = c(length(gblup_models), length(ann_models)),
  Model_trait_split_results = c(nrow(gblup_results), nrow(ann_results)),
  GEBV_records = c(nrow(gblup_predictions), nrow(ann_predictions)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

input_summary |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    caption = "Cross-validation predictions and performance records by model family",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
  )
```

```{r ranking-input-counts}
ranking_input_summary <- data.frame(
  Family = c("GBLUP", "ANN"),
  Individuals_per_trait_model = length(comparison_cv$ids),
  Ranking_records = c(nrow(gblup_ranking), nrow(ann_ranking)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  ranking_input_summary, format = "html", row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Stored individual OOF ranking records",
  table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
)
```

The expected combined dimensions are 525 split-level results,
20,475 individual held-out predictions and 4,095 individual ranking
records. These totals describe different units of observation and
must not be interpreted as independent biological replicates.

### 2.5 Matched outer tasks and assessment individuals

Cross-model matching uses the model-independent keys
`Trait`, `Repetition`, `Fold` and `SplitID`. The individual
identifier `ID` is added when matching predictions. The original
TaskID is not used because its definition differs across the fitting
modules.

The stored R03 outer assignment table is crossed with the three
traits to obtain the expected assessment keys for one model. Its
distinct split keys define the expected result records.

```{r comparison-expected-keys}
result_keys <- c("Trait", "Repetition", "Fold", "SplitID")
comparison_keys <- c(result_keys, "ID")

expected_prediction_keys <- merge(
  data.frame(Trait = traits, stringsAsFactors = FALSE),
  comparison_assessment,
  by = NULL
)
expected_prediction_keys <- expected_prediction_keys[
  , comparison_keys, drop = FALSE
]

expected_result_keys <- unique(expected_prediction_keys[
  , result_keys, drop = FALSE
])
```

The next tables distinguish duplicate keys, absent expected records
and unexpected records. Matching is performed on distinct keys so
that duplicates cannot inflate the number of matched records.
The expected counts are 75 distinct result keys and 2,925 distinct
prediction keys per model. Duplicate, missing and unexpected counts
should all be zero.

```{r comparison-key-coverage}
result_key_coverage <- data.frame()
prediction_key_coverage <- data.frame()
assessment_coverage <- data.frame()

for (model_name in model_order) {
  if (model_name %in% gblup_models) {
    model_results <- gblup_results[gblup_results$Model == model_name, , drop = FALSE]
    model_predictions <- gblup_predictions[gblup_predictions$Model == model_name, , drop = FALSE]
  } else {
    model_results <- ann_results[ann_results$Model == model_name, , drop = FALSE]
    model_predictions <- ann_predictions[ann_predictions$Model == model_name, , drop = FALSE]
  }

  observed_result_keys <- unique(model_results[, result_keys, drop = FALSE])
  observed_prediction_keys <- unique(model_predictions[, comparison_keys, drop = FALSE])

  matched_result_keys <- merge(
    expected_result_keys, observed_result_keys, by = result_keys
  )
  matched_prediction_keys <- merge(
    expected_prediction_keys, observed_prediction_keys, by = comparison_keys
  )

  result_key_coverage <- rbind(result_key_coverage, data.frame(
    Model = model_name,
    Records = nrow(model_results),
    Distinct_keys = nrow(observed_result_keys),
    Duplicate_keys = nrow(model_results) - nrow(observed_result_keys),
    Missing_keys = nrow(expected_result_keys) - nrow(matched_result_keys),
    Unexpected_keys = nrow(observed_result_keys) - nrow(matched_result_keys),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  ))

  prediction_key_coverage <- rbind(prediction_key_coverage, data.frame(
    Model = model_name,
    Records = nrow(model_predictions),
    Distinct_keys = nrow(observed_prediction_keys),
    Duplicate_keys = nrow(model_predictions) - nrow(observed_prediction_keys),
    Missing_keys = nrow(expected_prediction_keys) - nrow(matched_prediction_keys),
    Unexpected_keys = nrow(observed_prediction_keys) - nrow(matched_prediction_keys),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  ))

  # Count assessment records in each trait-by-split task.
  task_sizes <- aggregate(
    list(N = rep(1L, nrow(model_predictions))),
    by = model_predictions[, result_keys, drop = FALSE], FUN = sum
  )
  # Count predictions per individual and repetition, separately by trait.
  repetition_sizes <- aggregate(
    list(N = rep(1L, nrow(model_predictions))),
    by = model_predictions[, c("Trait", "ID", "Repetition")], FUN = sum
  )
  individual_sizes <- aggregate(
    list(N = rep(1L, nrow(model_predictions))),
    by = model_predictions[, c("Trait", "ID")], FUN = sum
  )

  assessment_coverage <- rbind(assessment_coverage, data.frame(
    Model = model_name,
    Tasks = nrow(task_sizes),
    Min_assessment_N = min(task_sizes$N),
    Max_assessment_N = max(task_sizes$N),
    Trait_individuals = nrow(individual_sizes),
    Min_OOF_N = min(individual_sizes$N),
    Max_OOF_N = max(individual_sizes$N),
    Repetition_groups = nrow(repetition_sizes),
    Non_single_repetition_groups = sum(repetition_sizes$N != 1L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  ))
}

knitr::kable(
  result_key_coverage, format = "html", row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Result-key coverage relative to the R03 design",
  table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
)
```

```{r display-prediction-key-coverage}
knitr::kable(
  prediction_key_coverage, format = "html", row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Individual assessment-key coverage relative to the R03 design",
  table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
)
```

The coverage counts should be read together with the next table:
each model should have 75 tasks of 39 predictions, 585
trait-individual groups with five OOF predictions each, and 2,925
trait-individual-repetition groups with one prediction each.
The key comparisons above also account for missing groups, which
cannot be identified from observed group sizes alone.

```{r display-assessment-coverage}
knitr::kable(
  assessment_coverage, format = "html", row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Assessment sample sizes and repeated OOF prediction coverage",
  table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
) |>
  kableExtra::scroll_box(width = "100%")
```

### 2.6 Matched BLUP targets across models

GBLUP-A is used only as a reference for checking the equality of
phenotypic BLUP targets, not as a preferred prediction method.
After matching on the individual assessment keys, the maximum
absolute BLUP difference measures target agreement. Full agreement
requires complete, unique keys (Section 2.5), finite targets and
zero difference for every matched record.

```{r matched-blup-targets}
comparison_keys <- c("Trait", "Repetition", "Fold", "SplitID", "ID")

blup_check <- gblup_predictions[
  gblup_predictions$Model == "GBLUP_A",
  c(comparison_keys, "BLUP"),
  drop = FALSE
]

target_match <- data.frame(
  Model = character(0),
  Matched_records = integer(0),
  Maximum_BLUP_difference = numeric(0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (model_name in model_order) {

  if (model_name %in% gblup_models) {

    model_predictions <- gblup_predictions[
      gblup_predictions$Model == model_name,
      c(comparison_keys, "BLUP"),
      drop = FALSE
    ]

  } else {

    model_predictions <- ann_predictions[
      ann_predictions$Model == model_name,
      c(comparison_keys, "BLUP"),
      drop = FALSE
    ]
  }

  matched <- merge(
    blup_check,
    model_predictions,
    by = comparison_keys,
    suffixes = c("_Check", "_Model"),
    all = FALSE,
    sort = FALSE
  )

  maximum_difference <- max(abs(matched$BLUP_Check - matched$BLUP_Model))

  target_match <- rbind(
    target_match,
    data.frame(
      Model = model_name,
      Matched_records = nrow(matched),
      Maximum_BLUP_difference = maximum_difference,
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  )
}

```

```{r display-blup-alignment}
target_match$Model <- factor(target_match$Model, levels = model_order, labels = model_labels)

target_match |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    digits = 12,
    caption = "BLUP alignment across the seven genomic models",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
  )
```

The target-alignment table reports the number of matched records
and the maximum difference. Its values must be interpreted alongside
the key-coverage tables rather than as evidence of completeness
from an inner join alone.

## 3. Evaluation metrics

### 3.1 Association and prediction error within an outer split

Let \(y_i\) denote the phenotypic BLUP and \(\widehat y_i\) the
stored genomic prediction for held-out individual \(i\). Each
assessment split contains \(n=39\) individuals.

| Metric | Interpretation | Reference direction |
|:-------|:---------------|:--------------------|
| Pearson | Linear association | Higher |
| Spearman | Rank association | Higher |
| RMSE | Quadratic prediction error | Lower |
| MAE | Absolute prediction error | Lower |
| Bias | Mean signed prediction error | Near zero |
| Slope | Calibration of predicted scale | Near one |

Pearson correlation measures linear association:

\[
r=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\bar y)(\widehat y_i-\overline{\widehat y})}
{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\bar y)^2
\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\widehat y_i-\overline{\widehat y})^2}}.
\]

Spearman correlation is Pearson correlation applied to the ranks
of observed and predicted values, using average ranks for ties.
A high correlation does not establish equality of predictions and
targets or absence of systematic error.

The error metrics on the original BLUP scale are

\[
\operatorname{RMSE}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\widehat y_i-y_i)^2},
\qquad
\operatorname{MAE}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\widehat y_i-y_i|.
\]

RMSE gives larger errors greater weight than MAE. Both are expressed
on the scale of the trait, so error magnitudes should be compared
within traits, not pooled across traits with different scales.

The stored fitting procedures return undefined correlations when
observed or predicted values are constant. Finite RMSE and MAE
remain meaningful in these cases. Section 4 distinguishes the
model-specific available splits from the common finite splits
used in direct correlation comparisons.

### 3.2 Complementary calibration metrics

Mean signed prediction error is defined as

\[
\operatorname{Bias}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\widehat y_i-y_i).
\]

Positive bias indicates average overprediction; negative bias
indicates underprediction. Bias near zero can result from
cancellation of positive and negative errors.

The calibration slope is the prediction coefficient in a regression
with an intercept:

\[
y_i=\alpha+\beta\widehat y_i+\varepsilon_i.
\]

The reference slope is one. With a meaningful positive association,
a slope greater than one can indicate insufficient dispersion of
predicted values, and a slope below one can indicate excessive
dispersion. A slope near one alone does not demonstrate calibration
of location or small errors. R04A stores an undefined slope when predictions are constant;
R04B also requires variation in the observed values. The stored
values are retained without recalculating calibration.

The following table summarizes the stored bias and slope across
each trait and model. Only finite values enter the means and sample
standard deviations; the counts show the number of contributing
splits. The slope means are model-specific available-split summaries,
not common-split contrasts. The four primary metrics and the
original comparison objects in Section 4 remain unchanged.

```{r complementary-calibration-summary}
calibration_summary <- data.frame()

for (trait in traits) {
  for (model_name in model_order) {
    if (model_name %in% gblup_models) {
      calibration_data <- gblup_results[
        gblup_results$Trait == trait & gblup_results$Model == model_name,
        , drop = FALSE
      ]
    } else {
      calibration_data <- ann_results[
        ann_results$Trait == trait & ann_results$Model == model_name,
        , drop = FALSE
      ]
    }

    bias_values <- calibration_data$Bias[is.finite(calibration_data$Bias)]
    slope_values <- calibration_data$Slope[is.finite(calibration_data$Slope)]

    calibration_summary <- rbind(calibration_summary, data.frame(
      Trait = trait,
      Model = model_name,
      Splits = nrow(calibration_data),
      Bias_N = length(bias_values),
      Bias = mean(bias_values),
      Bias_SD = sd(bias_values),
      Slope_N = length(slope_values),
      Slope = mean(slope_values),
      Slope_SD = sd(slope_values),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    ))
  }
}

knitr::kable(
  calibration_summary, format = "html", digits = 4, row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Complementary bias and calibration slope on available outer splits",
  table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
) |>
  kableExtra::scroll_box(width = "100%")
```

### 3.3 Aggregation and individual ranking

The split-level metrics are calculated before aggregation.
For metric \(M\), let \(\mathcal{S}_M\) denote the contributing
outer splits. With finite values in those splits, the mean is

\[
\overline M=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}_M|}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{S}_M}M_k.
\]

The mean split correlation is not a correlation calculated after
pooling all held-out predictions, and mean split RMSE is generally
different from pooled RMSE. Standard deviations describe variability
across dependent splits; they are not standard errors or confidence
intervals. No \(R^2\) metric is used.

For the individual ranking, the stored OOF predictions are averaged
over the five repetitions. Global Spearman correlation, absolute
rank error and recovery of the 39 highest observed BLUPs evaluate
different aspects of individual ordering. Descending ordering does
not necessarily correspond to the biologically favorable direction
for every trait.

Pairwise linearly weighted Cohen's kappa compares the ordered
GEBV-ranking strata between two prediction models, rather than
comparing predictions with BLUP targets. The intended quintile size
is 39 individuals. The construction of the groups and the
agreement measures are addressed in Section 6.

## 4. BLUP-GEBV performance across outer splits

The object `all_results` concatenates the 225 GBLUP and 300 ANN assessments after the shared metric names have been aligned. No assessment predictions are pooled across different outer splits.

### 4.1 Combined result object

```{r combined-results}
analysis_columns <- c(
  "Dataset",
  "Trait",
  "Repetition",
  "Fold",
  "SplitID",
  "Model",
  "Pearson",
  "Spearman",
  "RMSE",
  "MAE",
  "Bias",
  "Slope"
)

all_results <- rbind(gblup_results[, analysis_columns], ann_results[, analysis_columns])

rownames(all_results) <- NULL

```

The object `model_split_structure` counts the three traits, 25 outer splits per trait, and 75 assessments for each of the seven genomic models.

```{r evaluate-model-coverage}
model_split_structure <- data.frame(
  Model = character(0),
  Traits = integer(0),
  Outer_splits_per_trait = integer(0),
  Model_trait_split_results = integer(0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (model_name in model_order) {

  x <- all_results[all_results$Model == model_name,, drop = FALSE]

  split_counts <- table(x$Trait)

  model_split_structure <- rbind(
    model_split_structure,
    data.frame(
      Model = model_name,
      Traits = length(unique(x$Trait)),
      Outer_splits_per_trait = min(split_counts),
      Model_trait_split_results = nrow(x),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  )
}

model_split_structure$Model <- factor(
  model_split_structure$Model,
  levels = model_order,
  labels = model_labels
)

model_split_structure |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    caption = "Common outer-split evaluation structure by model",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
  )
```

### 4.2 Mean performance by trait and model

```{r performance-summary}
# Record the mean, standard deviation, and finite-fold count for each metric.
performance_summary <- data.frame(
  Model = character(0),
  Trait = character(0),
  Splits = integer(0),
  Pearson_N = integer(0),
  Pearson = numeric(0),
  Pearson_SD = numeric(0),
  Spearman_N = integer(0),
  Spearman = numeric(0),
  Spearman_SD = numeric(0),
  RMSE_N = integer(0),
  RMSE = numeric(0),
  RMSE_SD = numeric(0),
  MAE_N = integer(0),
  MAE = numeric(0),
  MAE_SD = numeric(0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (model_name in model_order) {

  for (trait in traits) {

    x <- all_results[all_results$Model == model_name & all_results$Trait == trait,, drop = FALSE]

    performance_summary <- rbind(
      performance_summary,
      data.frame(
        Model = model_name,
        Trait = trait,
        Splits = nrow(x),
        Pearson_N = sum(is.finite(x$Pearson)),
        Pearson = mean(x$Pearson, na.rm = TRUE),
        Pearson_SD = sd(x$Pearson, na.rm = TRUE),
        Spearman_N = sum(is.finite(x$Spearman)),
        Spearman = mean(x$Spearman, na.rm = TRUE),
        Spearman_SD = sd(x$Spearman, na.rm = TRUE),
        RMSE_N = sum(is.finite(x$RMSE)),
        RMSE = mean(x$RMSE, na.rm = TRUE),
        RMSE_SD = sd(x$RMSE, na.rm = TRUE),
        MAE_N = sum(is.finite(x$MAE)),
        MAE = mean(x$MAE, na.rm = TRUE),
        MAE_SD = sd(x$MAE, na.rm = TRUE),
        stringsAsFactors = FALSE
      )
    )
  }
}

```

The object `performance_summary` aggregates Pearson, Spearman, RMSE, and MAE over the outer assessments. `Pearson_N` and `Spearman_N` identify how many splits yield finite correlation values for each model and trait.

```{r display-performance-summary}
performance_summary$Trait <- factor(performance_summary$Trait, levels = traits)

performance_summary$Model <- factor(performance_summary$Model, levels = model_order)

performance_summary <- performance_summary[
  order(performance_summary$Trait, performance_summary$Model),
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]

performance_summary$Trait <- as.character(performance_summary$Trait)

performance_summary$Model <- as.character(performance_summary$Model)

PERFORMANCE_SUMMARY_CSV <- file.path(COMPARISON_DIR, "real_model_performance_summary.csv")

performance_display <- performance_summary[
  ,
  c("Model", "Trait", "Pearson_N", "Pearson", "Spearman_N", "Spearman", "RMSE", "MAE")
]

performance_display$Model <- factor(performance_display$Model, levels = model_order, labels = model_labels)

performance_display |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    digits = 4,
    caption = "Mean BLUP-GEBV performance across the 25 outer splits",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
  )
```

```{r save-performance-summary, eval=FALSE}
write.csv(performance_summary, PERFORMANCE_SUMMARY_CSV, row.names = FALSE)
```

Pearson and Spearman are summarized from all outer splits where the respective
correlation is defined. RMSE and MAE remain defined for every model-trait-split
combination.

### 4.3 Common finite splits for direct correlation comparison

When a model produces a constant prediction in an outer split, Pearson and
Spearman are undefined for that split. The descriptive model summaries above
retain every finite value available for each model. A direct cross-model
comparison, however, should use the same outer splits for all seven models.

For each trait and correlation metric, the following block therefore identifies
the intersection of outer splits where that metric is finite for all seven
models. Mean Pearson and Spearman values used to identify the best correlation
model are calculated only on these common finite splits. No split is removed
from RMSE or MAE comparisons because those metrics are defined in all 25 outer
splits.

```{r common-finite-correlation-splits}
# Separate model-specific finite estimates from matched finite-split comparisons.
common_correlation_summary <- data.frame(
  Model = character(0),
  Trait = character(0),
  Pearson_Common_N = integer(0),
  Pearson_Common = numeric(0),
  Spearman_Common_N = integer(0),
  Spearman_Common = numeric(0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (trait in traits) {

  trait_results <- all_results[all_results$Trait == trait,, drop = FALSE]

  split_ids <- sort(unique(trait_results$SplitID))

  pearson_common_splits <- character(0)
  spearman_common_splits <- character(0)

  for (split_id in split_ids) {

    split_data <- trait_results[trait_results$SplitID == split_id,, drop = FALSE]

    if (all(is.finite(split_data$Pearson))) {
      pearson_common_splits <- c(pearson_common_splits, split_id)
    }

    if (all(is.finite(split_data$Spearman))) {
      spearman_common_splits <- c(spearman_common_splits, split_id)
    }
  }

  for (model_name in model_order) {

    pearson_values <- trait_results$Pearson[
      trait_results$Model == model_name & trait_results$SplitID %in% pearson_common_splits
    ]

    spearman_values <- trait_results$Spearman[
      trait_results$Model == model_name & trait_results$SplitID %in% spearman_common_splits
    ]

    common_correlation_summary <- rbind(
      common_correlation_summary,
      data.frame(
        Model = model_name,
        Trait = trait,
        Pearson_Common_N = length(pearson_common_splits),
        Pearson_Common = mean(pearson_values),
        Spearman_Common_N = length(spearman_common_splits),
        Spearman_Common = mean(spearman_values),
        stringsAsFactors = FALSE
      )
    )
  }
}

```

For each trait, `common_correlation_summary` reports Pearson and Spearman means calculated from the intersection of outer splits with finite correlations for all seven models. The counts can differ by trait.

```{r display-common-finite-correlations}
COMMON_CORRELATION_SUMMARY_CSV <- file.path(COMPARISON_DIR, "real_model_common_split_correlation_summary.csv")

common_correlation_display <- common_correlation_summary
common_correlation_display$Model <- factor(
  common_correlation_display$Model,
  levels = model_order,
  labels = model_labels
)

common_correlation_display |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    digits = 4,
    caption = "Pearson and Spearman means on outer splits common and finite across all seven models",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
  )
```

```

### 4.4 Predictive winners by trait

The next table identifies the highest mean correlation and lowest mean
BLUP-GEBV error separately. It is a descriptive summary rather than a rule for
collapsing the seven models into a single winner.

```{r predictive-winners}
predictive_winners <- data.frame(
  Trait = character(0),
  Pearson_Common_N = integer(0),
  Best_Pearson_Model = character(0),
  Best_Pearson = numeric(0),
  Spearman_Common_N = integer(0),
  Best_Spearman_Model = character(0),
  Best_Spearman = numeric(0),
  Best_RMSE_Model = character(0),
  Best_RMSE = numeric(0),
  Best_MAE_Model = character(0),
  Best_MAE = numeric(0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (trait in traits) {

  x <- performance_summary[performance_summary$Trait == trait,, drop = FALSE]

  correlation_x <- common_correlation_summary[common_correlation_summary$Trait == trait,, drop = FALSE]

  pearson_index <- which.max(correlation_x$Pearson_Common)

  spearman_index <- which.max(correlation_x$Spearman_Common)

  rmse_index <- which.min(x$RMSE)

  mae_index <- which.min(x$MAE)

  predictive_winners <- rbind(
    predictive_winners,
    data.frame(
      Trait = trait,
      Pearson_Common_N = unique(correlation_x$Pearson_Common_N),
      Best_Pearson_Model = correlation_x$Model[pearson_index],
      Best_Pearson = correlation_x$Pearson_Common[pearson_index],
      Spearman_Common_N = unique(correlation_x$Spearman_Common_N),
      Best_Spearman_Model = correlation_x$Model[spearman_index],
      Best_Spearman = correlation_x$Spearman_Common[spearman_index],
      Best_RMSE_Model = x$Model[rmse_index],
      Best_RMSE = x$RMSE[rmse_index],
      Best_MAE_Model = x$Model[mae_index],
      Best_MAE = x$MAE[mae_index],
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  )
}

```

The object `predictive_winners` identifies the models with the highest common-split Pearson and Spearman correlations and the lowest RMSE and MAE for each trait.

```{r display-predictive-winners}

    format = "html",
    digits = 4,
    caption = "Best predictive metric by trait; correlations use common finite outer splits across all seven models",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
  ) |>
  kableExtra::scroll_box(width = "100%")
```

## 5. Matched ANN-versus-GBLUP outer-split contrasts

The seven models share the same outer splits, so every ANN variant can be
contrasted directly with every GBLUP structure within the same trait and split.

For Pearson and Spearman, positive values below indicate stronger BLUP-GEBV
association for the ANN. For RMSE and MAE, the contrast is defined as
`GBLUP - ANN`, so positive values indicate smaller BLUP-GEBV error for the ANN.
Correlation contrasts use only splits where both models have a finite value for
that metric.

```{r matched-family-contrasts}
split_keys <- c("Repetition", "Fold", "SplitID")

# Calculate matched ANN-minus-GBLUP advantages for all model-family pairs.
paired_summary <- data.frame(
  Trait = character(0),
  GBLUP = character(0),
  ANN = character(0),
  Pearson_N = integer(0),
  Mean_Pearson_Advantage = numeric(0),
  Spearman_N = integer(0),
  Mean_Spearman_Advantage = numeric(0),
  RMSE_N = integer(0),
  Mean_RMSE_Advantage = numeric(0),
  MAE_N = integer(0),
  Mean_MAE_Advantage = numeric(0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (trait in traits) {

  for (gblup_model in gblup_models) {

    for (ann_model in ann_models) {

      g <- all_results[
        all_results$Trait == trait & all_results$Model == gblup_model,
        c(split_keys, "Pearson", "Spearman", "RMSE", "MAE"),
        drop = FALSE
      ]

      a <- all_results[
        all_results$Trait == trait & all_results$Model == ann_model,
        c(split_keys, "Pearson", "Spearman", "RMSE", "MAE"),
        drop = FALSE
      ]

      matched <- merge(a, g, by = split_keys, suffixes = c("_ANN", "_GBLUP"), all = FALSE, sort = FALSE)

      pearson_finite <- is.finite(matched$Pearson_ANN) & is.finite(matched$Pearson_GBLUP)

      spearman_finite <- is.finite(matched$Spearman_ANN) & is.finite(matched$Spearman_GBLUP)

      rmse_finite <- is.finite(matched$RMSE_ANN) & is.finite(matched$RMSE_GBLUP)

      mae_finite <- is.finite(matched$MAE_ANN) & is.finite(matched$MAE_GBLUP)

      paired_summary <- rbind(
        paired_summary,
        data.frame(
          Trait = trait,
          GBLUP = gblup_model,
          ANN = ann_model,
          Pearson_N = sum(pearson_finite),
          Mean_Pearson_Advantage = mean(
              matched$Pearson_ANN[
                pearson_finite
              ] - matched$Pearson_GBLUP[pearson_finite]
            ),
          Spearman_N = sum(spearman_finite),
          Mean_Spearman_Advantage = mean(
              matched$Spearman_ANN[
                spearman_finite
              ] - matched$Spearman_GBLUP[spearman_finite]
            ),
          RMSE_N = sum(rmse_finite),
          Mean_RMSE_Advantage = mean(matched$RMSE_GBLUP[rmse_finite] - matched$RMSE_ANN[rmse_finite]),
          MAE_N = sum(mae_finite),
          Mean_MAE_Advantage = mean(matched$MAE_GBLUP[mae_finite] - matched$MAE_ANN[mae_finite]),
          stringsAsFactors = FALSE
        )
      )
    }
  }
}

```

The object `paired_summary` contains 36 contrasts: three traits, three GBLUP structures, and four ANN variants. Each contrast is calculated within matched outer splits; positive advantages favour ANN under the metric-specific sign convention stated above.

```{r display-matched-contrasts}
PAIRED_SUMMARY_CSV <- file.path(COMPARISON_DIR, "real_ann_vs_gblup_matched_summary.csv")

paired_summary |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    digits = 4,
    caption = "Matched ANN-versus-GBLUP mean performance advantage; positive values favor ANN",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
  ) |>
  kableExtra::scroll_box(width = "100%")
```

```{r save-matched-contrasts, eval=FALSE}
write.csv(paired_summary, PAIRED_SUMMARY_CSV, row.names = FALSE)
```

These paired contrasts summarize the direction and magnitude of differences
within the common outer cross-validation procedure. They are not interpreted as
independent-replicate significance tests.

## 6. Global ranking

The object `all_ranking` contains 4,095 model–trait–individual records. Each model contributes 195 individuals for each of the three traits.

### 6.1 Combined individual ranking object

```{r combined-ranking}
ranking_columns <- c(
  "Model",
  "Trait",
  "ID",
  "BLUP",
  "GEBV",
  "GEBV_SD",
  "BLUP_Rank",
  "GEBV_Rank",
  "Rank_Difference",
  "Absolute_Rank_Error",
  "BLUP_Top20",
  "GEBV_Top20"
)

all_ranking <- rbind(gblup_ranking[, ranking_columns], ann_ranking[, ranking_columns])

rownames(all_ranking) <- NULL

```

The objects `gblup_ranking` and `ann_ranking` contain the GEBVs calculated
from five held-out predictions per individual, trait, and model in R04A and
R04B. The object `all_ranking` combines those individual records without
recalculating their means.

### 6.2 Ranking summary

```{r ranking-summary}
# Compare the 195-individual rankings after aggregating five held-out predictions.
ranking_summary <- data.frame(
  Model = character(0),
  Trait = character(0),
  Individuals = integer(0),
  Ranking_Spearman = numeric(0),
  Mean_Absolute_Rank_Error = numeric(0),
  Median_Absolute_Rank_Error = numeric(0),
  Top20_N = integer(0),
  Top20_Overlap_N = integer(0),
  Top20_Overlap_Rate = numeric(0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (model_name in model_order) {

  for (trait in traits) {

    x <- all_ranking[all_ranking$Model == model_name & all_ranking$Trait == trait,, drop = FALSE]

    overlap_n <- sum(x$BLUP_Top20 & x$GEBV_Top20)

    ranking_summary <- rbind(
      ranking_summary,
      data.frame(
        Model = model_name,
        Trait = trait,
        Individuals = nrow(x),
        Ranking_Spearman = cor(x$BLUP_Rank, x$GEBV_Rank, method = "spearman"),
        Mean_Absolute_Rank_Error = mean(x$Absolute_Rank_Error),
        Median_Absolute_Rank_Error = median(x$Absolute_Rank_Error),
        Top20_N = 39L,
        Top20_Overlap_N = overlap_n,
        Top20_Overlap_Rate = overlap_n / 39L,
        stringsAsFactors = FALSE
      )
    )
  }
}

```

The object `ranking_summary` compares global BLUP–GEBV rank correlation, absolute rank error, and the number of BLUP top-20% individuals recovered by GEBV rankings among all 195 individuals.

```{r display-ranking-summary}
ranking_summary$Trait <- factor(ranking_summary$Trait, levels = traits)

ranking_summary$Model <- factor(ranking_summary$Model, levels = model_order)

ranking_summary <- ranking_summary[order(ranking_summary$Trait, ranking_summary$Model),, drop = FALSE]

ranking_summary$Trait <- as.character(ranking_summary$Trait)

ranking_summary$Model <- as.character(ranking_summary$Model)

RANKING_SUMMARY_CSV <- file.path(COMPARISON_DIR, "real_model_ranking_summary.csv")

ranking_display <- ranking_summary
ranking_display$Model <- factor(ranking_display$Model, levels = model_order, labels = model_labels)

ranking_display |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    digits = 4,
    caption = "Global BLUP-GEBV ranking and top-20% selection",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
  ) |>
  kableExtra::scroll_box(width = "100%")
```

```{r save-ranking-summary, eval=FALSE}
write.csv(ranking_summary, RANKING_SUMMARY_CSV, row.names = FALSE)
```

Split-level Spearman and global ranking Spearman answer different questions.
Split-level Spearman evaluates BLUP-GEBV ranking agreement among the 39
assessment individuals in one outer split. Global ranking Spearman evaluates
BLUP-GEBV ranking agreement among all 195 individuals after the GEBV of each
individual is obtained from its five predictions.

### 6.3 Ranking winners by trait

```{r ranking-winners}
ranking_winners <- data.frame(
  Trait = character(0),
  Best_Ranking_Spearman_Model = character(0),
  Best_Ranking_Spearman = numeric(0),
  Best_Mean_Rank_Error_Model = character(0),
  Best_Mean_Rank_Error = numeric(0),
  Best_Top20_Model = character(0),
  Best_Top20_Overlap_N = integer(0),
  Best_Top20_Overlap_Rate = numeric(0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (trait in traits) {

  x <- ranking_summary[ranking_summary$Trait == trait,, drop = FALSE]

  ranking_index <- which.max(x$Ranking_Spearman)

  rank_error_index <- which.min(x$Mean_Absolute_Rank_Error)

  top20_index <- which.max(x$Top20_Overlap_Rate)

  ranking_winners <- rbind(
    ranking_winners,
    data.frame(
      Trait = trait,
      Best_Ranking_Spearman_Model = x$Model[ranking_index],
      Best_Ranking_Spearman = x$Ranking_Spearman[ranking_index],
      Best_Mean_Rank_Error_Model = x$Model[rank_error_index],
      Best_Mean_Rank_Error = x$Mean_Absolute_Rank_Error[rank_error_index],
      Best_Top20_Model = x$Model[top20_index],
      Best_Top20_Overlap_N = x$Top20_Overlap_N[top20_index],
      Best_Top20_Overlap_Rate = x$Top20_Overlap_Rate[top20_index],
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  )
}

```

The object `ranking_winners` identifies the strongest global ranking correlation, smallest mean rank error, and largest top-20% overlap for each trait. These selection criteria are kept separate.

### 6.4 Ranking comparison figures

```{r ranking-spearman-figure, fig.width=10.5, fig.height=5.8, fig.cap="Global Spearman correlation between the BLUP ranking and the GEBV ranking for the seven genomic models."}
ranking_plot <- ranking_summary

ranking_plot$Model <- factor(ranking_plot$Model, levels = rev(model_order), labels = rev(model_labels))

ranking_plot$Trait <- factor(ranking_plot$Trait, levels = traits)

)

) + geom_tile(

  )

### 6.5 Pairwise agreement among GEBV-ranking quintiles

Spearman correlation compares the ordering of BLUPs and GEBVs within each
model. A separate question is whether different genomic models assign the same
individuals to similar **selection strata** based on their GEBV rankings.

For each trait and model, the 195 individuals are ordered from the highest to
the lowest GEBV and divided into five ordered groups of exactly 39 individuals:

- quintile 1: ranks 1--39;
- quintile 2: ranks 40--78;
- quintile 3: ranks 79--117;
- quintile 4: ranks 118--156;
- quintile 5: ranks 157--195.

Pairwise agreement among these ordered GEBV-ranking quintiles is quantified
with **linearly weighted Cohen's kappa**. All 21 unordered pairs formed by the
seven genomic methods are evaluated individually within each trait. No method
family is pooled, averaged, or otherwise aggregated for this comparison.
Identical quintile assignments receive full weight, whereas disagreement
receives progressively smaller weight as the distance between quintiles
increases. This provides a chance-corrected measure of agreement in selection
strata rather than a second measure of exact rank-position displacement.

```{r pairwise-quintile-weighted-kappa}
# Allocate 195 individuals to five equal GEBV-ranking quintiles for each method.
all_ranking$GEBV_Quintile <- (
  (
    all_ranking$GEBV_Rank - 1L
  ) %/%
    39L
) + 1L

for (trait in traits) {

  for (model_name in model_order) {

    quintile_counts <- table(
      all_ranking$GEBV_Quintile[all_ranking$Trait == trait & all_ranking$Model == model_name]
    )

  }
}

```

Linear weights decrease from 1 for identical quintiles to 0 for quintiles four categories apart. The matrix `quintile_weights` assigns these values to all 25 pairs of quintile categories.

```{r compute-linear-quintile-weights}
quintile_levels <- seq_len(5L)

quintile_weights <- matrix(0, nrow = 5L, ncol = 5L)

for (row_index in quintile_levels) {

  for (column_index in quintile_levels) {

    quintile_weights[row_index, column_index] <- 1 - abs(
        row_index - column_index
      ) / 4
  }
}

```

For each trait, `kappa_summary` calculates linearly weighted Cohen's kappa, exact quintile agreement, and mean absolute quintile difference for each of the 21 unordered pairs of genomic models.

```{r compare-ranking-quintiles}
# Compare every pair of genomic models separately within each trait.
kappa_summary <- data.frame(
  Trait = character(0),
  Model_1 = character(0),
  Model_2 = character(0),
  Weighted_Kappa = numeric(0),
  Exact_Quintile_Agreement_Rate = numeric(0),
  Mean_Absolute_Quintile_Difference = numeric(0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (trait in traits) {

  for (model_1_index in seq_len(length(model_order) - 1L)) {

    for (model_2_index in seq(from = model_1_index + 1L, to = length(model_order))) {

      model_1 <- model_order[model_1_index]

      model_2 <- model_order[model_2_index]

      x <- all_ranking[
        all_ranking$Trait == trait & all_ranking$Model == model_1,
        c("ID", "GEBV_Quintile"),
        drop = FALSE
      ]

      y <- all_ranking[
        all_ranking$Trait == trait & all_ranking$Model == model_2,
        c("ID", "GEBV_Quintile"),
        drop = FALSE
      ]

      x <- x[order(x$ID),, drop = FALSE]

      y <- y[order(y$ID),, drop = FALSE]

      agreement_table <- table(
        factor(x$GEBV_Quintile, levels = quintile_levels),
        factor(y$GEBV_Quintile, levels = quintile_levels)
      )

      observed_proportion <- agreement_table / sum(agreement_table)

      row_marginal <- rowSums(observed_proportion)

      column_marginal <- colSums(observed_proportion)

      expected_proportion <- outer(row_marginal, column_marginal)

      observed_weighted_agreement <- sum(quintile_weights * observed_proportion)

      expected_weighted_agreement <- sum(quintile_weights * expected_proportion)

      weighted_kappa <- (
          observed_weighted_agreement - expected_weighted_agreement
        ) / (1 - expected_weighted_agreement)

      exact_quintile_agreement_rate <- mean(x$GEBV_Quintile == y$GEBV_Quintile)

      mean_absolute_quintile_difference <- mean(abs(x$GEBV_Quintile - y$GEBV_Quintile))

      kappa_summary <- rbind(
        kappa_summary,
        data.frame(
          Trait = trait,
          Model_1 = model_1,
          Model_2 = model_2,
          Weighted_Kappa = weighted_kappa,
          Exact_Quintile_Agreement_Rate = exact_quintile_agreement_rate,
          Mean_Absolute_Quintile_Difference = mean_absolute_quintile_difference,
          stringsAsFactors = FALSE
        )
      )
    }
  }
}

KAPPA_SUMMARY_CSV <- file.path(COMPARISON_DIR, "real_model_pairwise_quintile_weighted_kappa.csv")

kappa_summary |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    digits = 4,
    caption = "Linearly weighted Cohen's kappa for each pair of genomic methods based on GEBV-ranking quintiles",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
  ) |>
  kableExtra::scroll_box(width = "100%")
```

```{r pairwise-quintile-weighted-kappa-heatmap, fig.width=13, fig.height=8.5, fig.cap="Linearly weighted Cohen's kappa for every pair of the seven genomic methods based on GEBV-ranking quintiles. Each panel is a complete 7 by 7 pairwise matrix for one trait; no aggregation by model family is applied. Larger values indicate stronger agreement in selection strata."}
kappa_heatmap <- data.frame(
  Trait = character(0),
  Model_1 = character(0),
  Model_2 = character(0),
  Weighted_Kappa = numeric(0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (trait in traits) {

  for (model_1 in model_order) {

    for (model_2 in model_order) {

      if (model_1 == model_2) {

        kappa_value <- 1

      } else {

        pair_row <- kappa_summary[
          kappa_summary$Trait == trait & (
              (
                kappa_summary$Model_1 == model_1 & kappa_summary$Model_2 == model_2

          Trait = trait,
          Model_1 = model_1,
          Model_2 = model_2,
          Weighted_Kappa = kappa_value,
          stringsAsFactors = FALSE
        )

    }
  }
}

## 7. BLUP versus GEBV

The following figures compare the BLUP with the GEBV for each individual and
model. The GEBV is the mean of the five predictions available for that
individual and is the same value used in the global ranking.

```{r create-trait-blup-gebv-plot}
# Use the same axis limits for BLUP and GEBV within each trait.
make_blup_gebv_plot <- function(trait) {

  trait_data <- all_ranking[all_ranking$Trait == trait,, drop = FALSE]

  trait_data$Model <- factor(trait_data$Model, levels = model_order, labels = model_labels)

  axis_limits <- range(c(trait_data$BLUP, trait_data$GEBV), finite = TRUE)

  axis_padding <- diff(
    axis_limits
  ) * 0.04

  axis_limits <- c(axis_limits[1L] - axis_padding, axis_limits[2L] + axis_padding)

  p_blup_gebv <- ggplot(
    trait_data,
    aes(x = BLUP, y = GEBV, color = Model)
  ) + geom_abline(
      intercept = 0,
      slope = 1,
      linetype = 2
    ) + geom_point(
      alpha = 0.62,
      size = 1.35
    ) + facet_wrap(
      ~ Model,
      ncol = 4
    ) + coord_equal(
      xlim = axis_limits,
      ylim = axis_limits
    ) + scale_color_gdocs() + labs(
      x = "BLUP",
      y = "GEBV",
      color = NULL,
      title = paste("BLUP versus GEBV:", trait)
    ) + theme_gdocs() + theme(legend.position = "none")

  p_blup_gebv
}
```

## 8. Integrated interpretation

The split-level metrics and the global ranking metrics are interpreted
together. A model can have smaller BLUP-GEBV error while another produces a
better global ordering of individuals; these are distinct properties and are
not collapsed into a single composite score.

```{r interpretation-objects, include=FALSE}
cer_predictive <- predictive_winners[predictive_winners$Trait == "Cer",, drop = FALSE]

bm_predictive <- predictive_winners[predictive_winners$Trait == "BM",, drop = FALSE]

lp_predictive <- predictive_winners[predictive_winners$Trait == "LP",, drop = FALSE]

cer_ranking <- ranking_winners[ranking_winners$Trait == "Cer",, drop = FALSE]

bm_ranking <- ranking_winners[ranking_winners$Trait == "BM",, drop = FALSE]

lp_ranking <- ranking_winners[ranking_winners$Trait == "LP",, drop = FALSE]

cer_kappa <- kappa_summary[kappa_summary$Trait == "Cer",, drop = FALSE]

bm_kappa <- kappa_summary[kappa_summary$Trait == "BM",, drop = FALSE]

lp_kappa <- kappa_summary[kappa_summary$Trait == "LP",, drop = FALSE]

cer_kappa_max <- cer_kappa[which.max(cer_kappa$Weighted_Kappa),, drop = FALSE]

cer_kappa_min <- cer_kappa[which.min(cer_kappa$Weighted_Kappa),, drop = FALSE]

bm_kappa_max <- bm_kappa[which.max(bm_kappa$Weighted_Kappa),, drop = FALSE]

bm_kappa_min <- bm_kappa[which.min(bm_kappa$Weighted_Kappa),, drop = FALSE]

lp_kappa_max <- lp_kappa[which.max(lp_kappa$Weighted_Kappa),, drop = FALSE]

lp_kappa_min <- lp_kappa[which.min(lp_kappa$Weighted_Kappa),, drop = FALSE]
```

### 8.1 Cer

For Cer, the highest mean split-level Pearson correlation is obtained by
**`r cer_predictive$Best_Pearson_Model`**
(`r sprintf("%.4f", cer_predictive$Best_Pearson)`), while the lowest mean RMSE
is obtained by **`r cer_predictive$Best_RMSE_Model`**
(`r sprintf("%.4f", cer_predictive$Best_RMSE)`). At the individual level, the
highest global ranking Spearman is obtained by
**`r cer_ranking$Best_Ranking_Spearman_Model`**
(`r sprintf("%.4f", cer_ranking$Best_Ranking_Spearman)`), and the largest
BLUP top-20% recovery is `r cer_ranking$Best_Top20_Overlap_N` of 39
individuals. For the GEBV-ranking quintiles, the highest pairwise weighted
kappa is observed for **`r cer_kappa_max$Model_1` versus
`r cer_kappa_max$Model_2`**
(`r sprintf("%.4f", cer_kappa_max$Weighted_Kappa)`), whereas the lowest is
observed for **`r cer_kappa_min$Model_1` versus
`r cer_kappa_min$Model_2`**
(`r sprintf("%.4f", cer_kappa_min$Weighted_Kappa)`).

### 8.2 BM

For BM, the highest mean split-level Pearson correlation is obtained by
**`r bm_predictive$Best_Pearson_Model`**
(`r sprintf("%.4f", bm_predictive$Best_Pearson)`), while the lowest mean RMSE
is obtained by **`r bm_predictive$Best_RMSE_Model`**
(`r sprintf("%.4f", bm_predictive$Best_RMSE)`). The global ordering can differ
from the split-level result: the highest ranking Spearman is obtained by
**`r bm_ranking$Best_Ranking_Spearman_Model`**
(`r sprintf("%.4f", bm_ranking$Best_Ranking_Spearman)`), and the largest
top-20% recovery is `r bm_ranking$Best_Top20_Overlap_N` of 39 individuals.
For the GEBV-ranking quintiles, the highest pairwise weighted kappa is observed
for **`r bm_kappa_max$Model_1` versus `r bm_kappa_max$Model_2`**
(`r sprintf("%.4f", bm_kappa_max$Weighted_Kappa)`), whereas the lowest is
observed for **`r bm_kappa_min$Model_1` versus `r bm_kappa_min$Model_2`**
(`r sprintf("%.4f", bm_kappa_min$Weighted_Kappa)`).

### 8.3 LP

For LP, the highest mean split-level Pearson correlation is obtained by
**`r lp_predictive$Best_Pearson_Model`**
(`r sprintf("%.4f", lp_predictive$Best_Pearson)`), while the lowest mean RMSE
is obtained by **`r lp_predictive$Best_RMSE_Model`**
(`r sprintf("%.4f", lp_predictive$Best_RMSE)`). Global ranking is evaluated
separately: the highest ranking Spearman is obtained by
**`r lp_ranking$Best_Ranking_Spearman_Model`**
(`r sprintf("%.4f", lp_ranking$Best_Ranking_Spearman)`), and the largest
top-20% recovery is `r lp_ranking$Best_Top20_Overlap_N` of 39 individuals.
For the GEBV-ranking quintiles, the highest pairwise weighted kappa is observed
for **`r lp_kappa_max$Model_1` versus `r lp_kappa_max$Model_2`**
(`r sprintf("%.4f", lp_kappa_max$Weighted_Kappa)`), whereas the lowest is
observed for **`r lp_kappa_min$Model_1` versus `r lp_kappa_min$Model_2`**
(`r sprintf("%.4f", lp_kappa_min$Weighted_Kappa)`).

### 8.4 Overall interpretation

The comparison does not impose a universal winner. Predictive association,
BLUP-GEBV error, global ranking, recovery of superior individuals, and
pairwise agreement among GEBV-ranking quintiles are reported separately because
they represent different objectives in genomic prediction and selection.

For weighted kappa, interpretation is strictly **method by method**. Each cell
of the complete pairwise matrix represents one specific pair among GBLUP-A,
GBLUP-AD, GBLUP-ADE, ANN-0, ANN-L1, ANN-L2, and ANN-L1+L2. No average or
pooled contrast is calculated for a GBLUP family, an ANN family, or for a
GBLUP-versus-ANN grouping. The 21 method pairs are evaluated independently
within each trait.

All seven methods are evaluated under one common rule: identical outer splits,
identical BLUPs, no model-specific post-processing of individual folds, and
global ranking from the GEBV obtained for each individual from its five
predictions.
